utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I will ask the Registrar to call out the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Shall we start with Mr. Curtis -- honestly, I had no time to check the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have checked it, Your Honour, and I think, in all fairness to Mr. Fila, we can resolve this. I think what happened is, after I looked at the transcript, I believe Mr. Fila and I were both correct to some extent. Mr. Fila asked the question to Mr. Dokmanovic, he said: "What did you talk about during that meeting? What did they ask you? Well, not on that day. In general. In general." Then Mr. Dokmanovic replied in some detail as to the substance of what was said. When I was taking my notes, I wrote down what Mr. Dokmanovic said. But looking at the transcript, I'm not sure that Mr. Fila intended to elicit the response that he got from Mr. Dokmanovic when he asked the question in the way that he did. So as a result, I will not go into the substance of the interview with Mr. Curtis. However, should Mr. Fila wish to do so, then we would feel that we would be in a position to do so on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I didn't want to speak about that and I won't. I completely agree. I would like to ask Mr. Williamson something before we begin with Mr. Curtis. As I said, if you have nothing against this -- and Mr. Curtis can stay, because he is a professional, one of the professionals, so to speak, from our profession -- I have come by some documents that I'd like to hand around to you, which, generally speaking, one is an additional addendum to D1; if you remember, the meteorological report. That is an addendum which helps to throw better light on the picture and speaks of visibility. It's nothing special. I would just like you to have a look at it. It's just an addendum. That document was up for translation. We've received it now. So you can see it. It's nothing special, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe -- we have already received a copy of this previously in English. If Mr. Fila is offering this for introduction into evidence, we would have an objection to this as being beyond the expertise of a meteorologist to reach conclusions about how far away someone can see certain -- see faces. I just don't believe that that is within the expertise of a meteorologist, to offer opinions as to that issue. So we would object to it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, as you will. I've asked for it, I've received it, and here you are, because Judge Cassese asked for it. That's what I asked for, I got, and you can do what you like with it. I just wanted to be at the service of the Tribunal, if I can put it that way. Look at it later on, add it to Exhibit D1. If not, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had no objection to the original report which gave the times of sunset and sunrise and all of that. Our only objection is to these conclusions about how far away someone can see a face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I would share the views of the Prosecutor. Actually, what I had asked for was --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Very well. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I too believe -- I don't need to consult with my fellow Judges -- that this is a matter of admissibility within certain distance --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I propose something that I think we'll all agree to? If you take note that you do not need this, then take it just as if I hadn't put it forward. Never mind. I retract. No problem. I just wanted to do it as a service to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. It should be then given back to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The second document that I want to give you is from the sphere of an international conflict. They are new documents that I have come by. It is the Sabor or Parliament of the Republic of Croatia, the conclusions of the 28th of December, 1991, calling for the recognition of Croatia as an independent state. That is when recognition was requested. So may I tender that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D146.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have the original in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. So as not to encumber the minutes, this is a set of documents on the introduction of a new currency and the ceasing to exist of the dinar. There are a lot of documents, so this is a set of documents, and I propose to tender these as a set into evidence. And, of course, you can look at them individually. They all have to do with the dinar, which will no longer be in use, and the new currency that came into use after the dinar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: These are, Mr. Fila, documents relating to the issue of whether or not there was an international armed conflict --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, an international armed conflict. Only that. Like the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia was independent --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whether it was independent or not, yes. But there are a lot of documents. I have tendered them as a set. And they all relate to the same subject, currency, the dinar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The documents are marked D147.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, I believe each paper clip --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think each paper clip had all of one document because I got six copies of one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the one you saw -- all of them are more or less the same. So if you've seen one, you have more or less seen them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I was incorrect then. Maybe I didn't look at it thoroughly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are, of course, quite right, Mr. Williamson. As I say, they are more or less the same, mutatis mutandis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are receiving this document, I would like to apologise to Mr. Dokmanovic for not asking him today whether he can follow me in Serbian. Thank you, Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would now like to put forward a document when we complete this matter. Would the Usher hand this document around because I am sure the Prosecution will have something to say against it. So I want to hand it around on time. I would like to explain it, because I referred to it in my introduction, and I would like to have the court take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe I can again profit from this time, to save time, to say that we, yesterday, the members of the Trial Chamber, we have met once again, and I was asked by my colleagues to, in a way, warn you that we have now in June five days, from the 22nd to the 26th of June. On the 26th of June, the trial must be over. We must finish by the 26th of June. Therefore, this is particularly an appeal to the Prosecutor. If you need a lot of time for rebuttal witnesses, that means that we will shorten the time available to you for the closing statements. Therefore, make sure that we can use our time in a proper manner and that we'll finish by the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might address this just briefly? We certainly will do everything that we can to comply with the court's ruling. Our only concern is, if Mr. Fila's evidence goes over, that we are, in effect, punished for that if his takes longer than what he is anticipating. As long as his is brief, I think we should have no problem whatsoever completing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand from Mr. Fila that his witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's right. And if I find, and I hope to find an expert witness for the system of old Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but I'll be handing that in in writing, a written expert report in English. So, Mr. Williamson, I don't think I'll use up even two days of our time. But let's say two days. Of course, if you have questions, then I can -- what can I ask his wife? What kind of a husband he was. And what else can she say except that he was a good husband? I don't see that that will last long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you will need not more than two days. And the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would anticipate that we would need perhaps two and a half days at the most. I think we can complete it in two. I am saying that out of an abundance of caution. But, for example, if Mr. Fila's witness is going to be Mr. Dokmanovic's wife, I don't anticipate that we would have a lot of cross-examination. I think we might very well finish his witnesses in one day. I think those should go very quickly. If that's the case, then we certainly have plenty of time to do it. Your Honour, I had one other issue on this, though. If, after having seen our evidence, though, there were questions still in the court's mind as to the locations that are depicted on the videotape, we would make a motion that the court pay a visit to the scene. Again, the court may reject that out of hand. If that's the case, then so be it. But if that were the situation at that time -- I think it's entirely up to Your Honours. After you've seen the evidence, if you have questions, if you think it needs clarification, and that it would help for you to pay a visit to the scene, then we would certainly put that out as an option. I don't think that need be decided right now. I just want to let you know that that is a possibility, that we certainly would not oppose it, if you would desire to do so having heard the evidence. But, again, that may be something that you have no interest in doing, and this is entirely a matter up to the court, and it is your decision, and how it would affect the timetable is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask Mr. Fila how he would react to this suggestion by the Prosecutor over a visit to the place?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have absolutely nothing against because everything working in the interests of truth is all right by me. But I would like to react to something else at this point. First of all, I still have not received the declaration of war that Mr. Mesic mentioned. I still haven't heard an explanation why opposite evidence was given to me two minutes prior to the hearing, something that we were to discuss yesterday but we forgot. Third, why did I not get the minutes by Mr. Curtis, from Mr. Curtis, and Mr. Niemann promised to give me that when I was in Belgrade. I still have not got the minutes of that, and I am now to hear what Mr. Curtis said on the occasion. So I still haven't received the minutes. Fourth, will I have the possibility of giving my views on the evidence presented by the Prosecution in rebuttal without knowing what he is going to present in rebuttal? Because, if on the 26th, I hear the rebuttal by the Prosecutor, I am not a magician to be able to know what he has so that I can agree on the 23rd whether it is correct or not. And I'd like to draw the court's attention to something very vital. Mr. Dokmanovic did not make the tape himself, Mr. Dokmanovic did not have the tape, and you can see from all the minutes and records that he never mentioned the tape because he forgot all about the tape. It is witness Jevtovic who made the tape, as he says, and witness Lazarevic had the tape, and Dokmanovic never had the tape at all, never saw the tape. The Prosecutor did not ask Jevtovic where and when the tape was made, and witness Jevtovic just left without having been asked. Yes, you asked for the tape, Mr. Williamson. I can just make an error by chance but not expressly. You said how it was numbered, whether it was mounted, and so on and so forth, but he was not told that that was not the tape, to hear what the man would say. Therefore, I cannot accept anything of that rebuttal and to complete in a situation where I am being blackmailed. And so, please, if you promise me something, please keep your promises. I have no idea of Mr. Curtis's notes, what they are. I said -- I'm sorry. I am sure Mr. Curtis has his notes. He had them before, so why shouldn't he have them now? But the fact remains that I haven't received them. So ask and you will hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Before I give the floor to -- I ask Mr. Williamson to answer the various queries of Mr. Fila, may I say that we discussed briefly this suggestion of going to Vukovar to see the place, but, of course, we will decide probably in that week between the 22nd and 26th of June, and this, if we decide to go there, this, of course, should occur after that week, in the following week. I hope it would not take more than two or three days. Of course, the parties should go there. And I wonder whether there are any security problems, in particular for the accused, because I assume the accused also should be there. Let us now leave aside this problem because we will reconsider it in that particular week. Let's go back to the various issues raised by Mr. Fila. I think what he said is quite sensible, so I would like to ask Mr. Williamson to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, he raised a number of issues, so I'm not sure that I will recall all of them in addressing it. In relation to this declaration of war that Mr. Mesic had referred to, this is a document that apparently is at the United Nations. We have put in a request, we have made a follow-up request. We have not yet received it. We have been told that they are researching their records for it. There is nothing that I can do about that. We do not have it in our possession. It is not something that we are holding out and not giving over to him. We just simply do not have it. Mr. Mesic referred to it in his testimony. We have made attempts to obtain it, but we don't have it at this time. As soon as we do, we will forward it to the court. The next issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The problem is that the Defence considers that that document does not exist and that Mr. Mesic, quite simply, made it up. So I am quite satisfied if the Prosecution can tell me that no document of that kind exists, just to bear out what Mr. Mesic said. General Kadijevic is a Croatian General. How can a Croatian General declare war on Croatia? I have never heard anything of the kind. Quite illogical. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I asked the question on this issue to the witness, and it was very clear that this declaration of war was a misnomer. It was not a declaration of war because -- it's not, technically speaking, a declaration of war. It was a sort of warning, ultimatum, which cannot be classified as a declaration of war. It is most likely that the document does exist. You could probably, Mr. Williamson, ask again the U.N., relevant U.N. office, to send us this document, a copy of this document. It should be very easy for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In theory, it should be, yes. We all know there are some difficulties in dealing with the U.N. Again, Your Honour, how I reply to this, from Mr. Fila's statement, is that at the end of the day, the Tribunal will look at what evidence is before it and will make decisions as to what we have proved and what we have not proved. And if we fail to provide this, then is the appropriate time to reach a conclusion as to whether it exists or not. It is our obligation to provide it. We bear the burden of proof. If we don't do that, then you can decide appropriately. But to argue these issues right now and say that a decision should be reached one way or another, I think that's just premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What were the other points that I needed to address? In reference to the notes of Mr. Curtis, this gets into this bigger issue which Mr. Fila wanted to discuss about our obligation to turn over materials. In relation to the notes in particular, the position that we took, and I still stand by this as being appropriate, is that this was a work product, that we have the right to go and interview any person we want to. If notes are made on that, it is our internal work product. Rule 66A requires only that we turn over signed statements of Prosecution witnesses. That is the rule as it is written. It is explicit -- I believe, unless it has been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the notes are used as something that will be evidence. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: -- just one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just try to find out what's going on. What use do you want to make of the notes now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The use that we want to make of the notes at this time is Mr. Curtis will refer to them in his testimony. I am going to pose very limited questions to him, only on the issues wherein Mr. Novakovic's testimony differed from Mr. Curtis's version of events. To that extent, I will pose the questions to Mr. Curtis. If he needs to refer to his notes, that's fine. If Mr. Fila wishes these notes to be entered into evidence, we have no objection to that at this point. We feel that, however, they are largely irrelevant. They cover a number of issues of which there was no disagreement about; they cover some issues which no testimony was offered on. It is not a signed statement. It is the notes of Mr. Curtis. We have no problem with Mr. Fila having a chance to look at these, see what's in there, see if what he is testifying to is consistent with what's in the notes. If he wishes them to be entered into the record for the sake of completeness, we have no objection. In fact, we feel like it actually assists us. But again, the issue that we feel is before the court is what our obligations are under cross-examination. We have an obligation to turn over statements of our witnesses that we call. We have interviewed probably 50, 70 additional witnesses in relation to Vukovar that weren't called in this case for a variety of reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment now. You are now seeking to call a witness in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And at the moment, there is no document given to the Defence or before the court referring to that evidence. You are just calling him blind. You may know what he is going to say, or what you think he is going to say, but nobody else does. That's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think that I have laid out exactly what he will say during the course of questions that I put to Mr. Novakovic. Because I asked him specifically and said: Did you tell Mr. Curtis on this date this? Did you tell Mr. Curtis this? Those are the only questions that I will put to him. I am not going to go into any other areas, anything else that was discussed. So I think I've given adequate notice a month ago as to the questions that I would address to him. We made it clear at that time that anything that Mr. Novakovic disagreed with, we would call Mr. Curtis in rebuttal but only on those issues. So it's very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got, have you, photocopies of the relevant part of the notes, or can you obtain photocopies if we want them --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We have them in their entirety, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But if we wanted a part, the part that you are going to deal with, the relevant part, you could give us those?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The problem is, there were several issues and they are interspersed throughout the notes. What it would require is for us to then go through and redact everything else that is in the notes which, I mean, we can certainly do, but you will end up with probably ten pages of black Magic Marker and three or four lines. It's up to the court how you want to handle this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many pages are there in all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think in relation to Mr. Novakovic it's -- if I might put a question to Mr. Curtis for these purposes? Mr. Curtis, is this -- it's only Mr. Novakovic's notes that are included here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CURTIS
utterances.text: Can I just mention that I haven't been sworn in yet? But it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am just asking this, if you can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. It's 15 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is your objection in principle to Mr. Fila having those notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We have no objection to him having those notes and we are happy to give those to him. Our objection was that meant that we had an obligation to turn it over before cross-examination, which Mr. Fila was saying that we should have given over the statement of Mr. Licina before cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, let me interrupt. For the moment, that's a separate issue. What we have to decide at the moment is whether Mr. Fila is entitled to a copy of these notes now. At least as I understand it, that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's fine. We have no objection. I am happy to provide him with the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Williamson, therefore, we would like to receive the notes after redaction, and also, of course, Mr. Fila should also receive a copy of these notes after redaction, so that you take out all the points which are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. That will take some time. I can't do it right here in court. It would require at least 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have plenty of time in June to take a look at this, but I just wanted to say one thing, Your Honour. I got the notes from the meeting Mr. Curtis had with Mr. Dokmanovic, and we are not going to use that. I mean, I got that from the Office of the Prosecutor. I have already been given that once. But I asked, just as they gave me those notes from that conversation, because -- and we did not use that set of notes, Mr. Williamson and I agreed on that, and the same way I got those notes, I had requested these notes. So we already had a precedent, don't we? So I just protested, because last time Mr. Niemann said, because this is according to American procedure, that if the rebuttal is used with certain -- rebuttal proof is used with certain notes, the Defence should take a look at it so they could prepare themselves. So that is what I wish to say. And we can hear Mr. Curtis in June. It is not all that important if I get the notes and if I find these responses of Mr. Curtis's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: First of all, I think there is a clear distinction between a statement made by Mr. Dokmanovic. We gave over that to Mr. Fila because we felt obligated to give him any information we had regarding things that Mr. Dokmanovic had said. So I think there is a clear distinction between that situation and the one here. And in reply to what he said -- what Mr. Niemann said in court, and I will quote him directly from the transcript, he says: "They are not matters which are discoverable under the rules and, Your Honours, at the end of the day, if there are any notes made by the witness which he would rely upon for the purpose of his testimony, the appropriate time is then for Mr. Fila to call for them and say 'I want to inspect those notes,' and then they can be made available at that stage. It is inappropriate at the moment to be asking for them." Mr. Niemann did not say at any time that we would provide these in advance, he said at the time that he was testifying, and we are following that as it is written in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is in advance, before the witness starts to speak. That is what I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, all right. I think now we have reached an agreement whereby Mr. Williamson will kindly hand in the notes, redacted notes. However, I think it would be a waste of time to put off everything until June because, I mean, we still have time. I wonder whether we could discuss other matters while the redaction may be carried out. I wonder whether you yourself have got to redact those notes. Because if you could ask somebody else, then we could move on and discuss other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. It's not necessary for me to do it personally. Perhaps if Mr. Curtis can step out, and he knows exactly where they are in the notes, and along with Mr. Vos. They can do that. Again, I think that at the point that we actually start taking testimony from Mr. Curtis, it will only take 15 or 20 minutes. I think this will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I might just have a moment to give instructions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might also. There is, at the conclusion of the interviews that Mr. Curtis conducted, he prepared a typed report as well, which incorporates his notes. So we will also redact that. But during the course of this trip he interviewed, I believe, seven witnesses. So we will pull out the portion that refers to Mr. Novakovic and we will redact that portion alone, because some of the reports refer to Defence witnesses who did not testify in this matter. So we will remove everything else. We will have that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us now use our time also to address two other issues. First of all, what about the document which has been given by Mr. Fila? The set of documents, D147, I wonder whether the Prosecutor had a chance of glancing through these documents to say whether he objects to the tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't mean to interrupt. This is the set of documents that refer to the currency, the Dina. We would have no objection to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So it's D147. And it's a set of documents. All right. What about D148, the interview with Mr. Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We would have an objection to this one, as Mr. Fila predicted. It's an interview, an alleged interview that appears in a newspaper from Croatia. It's apparently -- it is certainly subject to editing. We have no way of knowing what Mr. Berghofer has said, and we would also object on the grounds of relevance. But this issue was raised in relation to an interview earlier, by Mr. Fila, that Dr. Wheeler gave after testifying. And after speaking with Dr. Wheeler, we determined that there were gross inaccuracies in the interview, and this is in the same publication. So, for that reason alone, we would object to its admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I think that I did not suggest Mr. Wheeler. As far as Mr. Wheeler's interview is concerned, let me be quite clear. I thought that it was not polite towards this court, and that is what I wrote, that experts make statements to the press and assess the work of the court. That was the problem, as far as Mr. Wheeler is concerned, not what he said. He's not supposed to speak -- to say that, "I prove that such and such a person is guilty and I ascertain this, I ascertain that." That's the problem with Mr. Wheeler, but I didn't ask for this to be evidence, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I again will take issue with that, because, I think, as we reported in our response to that, Dr. Wheeler did not make the statements that Mr. Fila is attributing to him. He did in fact give an interview. I don't think that there is anything that we can do, as an institution, to keep people from giving interviews. Perhaps lawyers, and certainly members of the Office of the Prosecutor, can have restrictions placed on them about giving interviews, but I'm not sure that there's much that we can do about other persons doing that. Perhaps there is, and it would probably be beneficial, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You could tell them, Mr. Williamson, not to give interviews, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Certainly, but we weren't anticipating this. We had no way of knowing. And I know, Judge May, from your jurisdiction there are very strict rules in relation to publication of ongoing cases, and I think that those would work better in my jurisdiction, if we had some of those restrictions. But, as I said, we don't have any of those restrictions in place right now. This was not an issue that we knew anything about in advance. The first time we found out about it was when we received the request from Mr. Fila. As I said, when we made inquiries with Dr. Wheeler, we determined that much of what was reported in the article was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In any case, it was absolutely inappropriate of Mr. Wheeler to give an interview. I think in future we will ask witnesses not to say anything about what happens here in court. This applies to both fact witnesses and expert witnesses, of course. Now, as for the -- let us now discuss this issue of Mr. Berghofer's interview. I'm afraid we can't admit this interview into evidence, because, of course, otherwise -- to check the veracity of what was said here, we would have to call the reporter and Mr. Berghofer. I think -- he should not have given this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. But I mentioned it in my opening statements, and I would have deemed it unprofessional had I not done what I did, because I mentioned him. And, according to our system, too, they are not allowed to make statements because this disqualifies them, witnesses and experts alike. So none of my witnesses have opened their mouths since the trial began.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate what Mr. Fila is saying, but I think this is, perhaps, a little bit inappropriate coming from him. Because Mr. Fila has made a number of comments to the press in regard to this case, and in regard to the Tribunal, and some of them which have been very critical of the working of the Tribunal. We have now raised this issue, but this is not a one-sided thing of our witnesses. If Mr. Fila feels very strongly about this, then I think the same rules should apply to him and what he is saying publicly about this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I say publicly -- I mean, you will have to prove that I said it. I never gave that interview, the one that you are referring to. And also -- I mean, in terms of the response you gave me. Never did I ever utter these words. And not even know, I don't see what this is talking about. I don't even know what you are talking about. What I said, on television, for example, in Banja Luka and in Baranja, next to me is Mr. Westendorp's censor, who would have turned off my microphone, had I said anything wrong. On the contrary, our opinions in Yugoslavia are such, and Mr. Casesse knows this, when he was President of the Tribunal, when I used to come here, there was the question of the legitimacy of this court, whether in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations, Chapter 7, whether it was legitimate to establish this court or not. But once this has been done it has been done. And that is what I kept saying in each and every one of the statements. The court is here now, and if this court were illegitimate, the members of the United Nations would have voted in favour of not having it exist, and no one protested. No one voted against the establishment of this court. So there. So what Sona writes? I mean, this is a war between news agencies and Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, the Sona agency says that Louise Arbour calls all our people criminals, that Serbs are 75 percent guilty, 20 percent Croats and five percent Muslims. And I know that that is incorrect, but that is what it says in those papers, you know. I am not complaining. I am just saying that expert witnesses should not make statements to the press after the trial, after testifying, and that they should not speak about their testimonies. And this is not allowed in my system either. Privately you can have an opinion about me, about anyone, and any kind of opinion you wish to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is just the inherent danger of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's not nice to bring me into this story, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I say that -- I mean, I'm sure that we all agree, first of all, that nobody should give interviews. And also, and this is the second point, because we all know reporters, they deform our thinking, our words, they put words into your mouth and so on. So this is further reason why everybody, from judges, prosecutors, defence counsel, witnesses and so on, must refrain from talking to the media. Because the media, I mean, are very keen to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the tape that I showed you as an alibi, the alibi tape, was never shown on Yugoslav television, but from here it was broadcast on Croatian television, you know. On Serb television it was never broadcast. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I mean it was so obvious, it was on television. Mr Waespipy has the tape. Let him tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think we have now to redact, because you should not have mentioned the testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- of a particular witness. All right. But I think the problem has been fleshed out now sufficiently and we can move on to an important matter, which is of great importance to us, namely, the submission by both parties now of the statements to be called in the final week. So the rebuttal witnesses and those witnesses Mr. Fila intends to call. We would like to give you a deadline. We would like to ask both parties to submit to each other, and to the court, all those statements by the 15th of June. So one week before the week when we start -- we resume our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wish to repeat one thing. I am going to hand in everything I have, and you know what you will be receiving, a few people who will be speaking about his character and also the expert witness. But, please, may I receive in good time rebuttal evidence so that I could get prepared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That's why I said 15th of June. 15th of June. I think -- I wonder whether the Prosecutor could -- do you need all the statements, witness statements in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It can be in English. It can be in Swahili, if you wish. Just give it to me. But I know what it's about, you know. Please, I cannot respond on the very same morning of the 15th of June. I should provide my own on the 15th, or by the 15th. But I have to get that from the Prosecutor before that, so that I can respond to his too, because I imagine that the Prosecutor is not going to respond to me, because there is nothing to respond about. I mean, I imagine that that is the case, but he has the right to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, what do you mean by respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know, you know, he has the right to rebuttal, and in terms of the evidence that I am going to present, but the evidence that I am going to present are really character witnesses in terms of Mr. Dokmanovic. So I don't really see, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So what is important is, as I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There has to be a different deadline for us, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What are you suggesting, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Until the 15th we need to give them to one another, and give me an additional five days in respect of what the Prosecutor proposes, so that then I can give possible rebuttal. So perhaps let us shorten the deadline. Let it be June 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, before you go into conference. I'm sorry. I think we may need until the 15th for some witnesses. We will certainly hand over anything that we get in advance of that. We will not wait until the 15th, if we have something available prior to then. But we are just concluding today, and we are going to have some expert analysis done, and I am not sure that we will have all of our reports available prior to then. Anything we do have available, as soon as we get it, we'll hand it over to the Defence, but we would like to keep the date of the 15th as a final deadline. Hopefully, everything can be handed over prior to that, but, if necessary, to go up to that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: First of all, may ask you, Mr. Williamson, what sort of evidence are you going to call? I mean, you spoke of rebuttal witnesses. Could you give us --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't tell you with complete specificity at this point. I mean, the case has just finished. We are still trying to analyze this. We will call several witnesses in relation to the issue of the videotape to establish the whereabouts of where that -- of exactly where we are saying this part that is depicted at 15.42 actually is. So the bulk of the testimony will be related to that. We probably will call one fact witness in relation to some of the things that were said during the course of Defence testimony, and perhaps one or two other experts on other areas. But, again, this is something that we are discussing, we are still trying to resolve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Nothing about the possible editing of the tape? No expert witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It may be, yes, Your Honour. But this is something that we have not been in a position to do up until now, because we had to hear the testimony before we can have someone go and tell us what -- whether this is consistent or inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are wondering, because, I mean, the tape was available to you, has been available for -- and Mr. Fila, actually, asked you, many times, to ask the Dutch police to make a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour. We went to the Dutch police, and we were told that with a copy of a tape, that they were not able to do any analysis on it, that in fact anything could be done with a copy, and they just did not feel in a position to do any analysis. Since that time we have made other inquiries, and at this time it appears that the FBI laboratory in the United States is in a position to do analysis on the tape that was not available to us from someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So, therefore, we must give time to the Defence to call experts and so on, if you are going to produce this sort of -- I would say that, in any case, we think that you should hand to the Defence all the relevant material, namely, the expert -- sorry, witness statements, by the 12th of June at 12.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. We'll comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So by Friday at 12. At least you have some more time. Whereas you, Mr. Fila, you would have until the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the 15th of June I am going to respond, and I don't have to receive the statements in Serbian at all. Oh, yes, yes, I can even give it earlier. It's very little, you know. No problem with me, you know. But, please, may this be rebuttal-proof, as Judge May said? Let us not introduce new evidence and let us not start giving completely new evidence once again. I hope I have understood the Prosecutor correctly, that this is rebuttal. I mean, not someone who did not come the first time and who was on that list and now introducing new witnesses. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly, the evidence that we are he presenting is largely in response to the alibi. Under no system, that I am aware of, would we be expected to rebut an alibi before it is actually presented. The bulk of what we will be presenting during this time relates to the alibi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis -- Mr. Williamson. I'm sorry. With regard to what you have just said. But I thought that the reason why the rules make it obligatory for the Defence to give notice of the alibi and all the evidence they are going to call for the alibi is precisely what you said, that the Prosecution should have time to investigate it and call their witnesses during the time that they are giving the Prosecution evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And on the tape -- the Prosecution were handed this tape. If it was a copy, you had enough time to ask for the original and things like that. So one wonders why you should do it in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. First of all, Your Honours, there is no original tape. There is no original. All that we have is a copy. The testimony was that the original was made on a mini-cassette, so the best copy we have is a first generation copy. So there was no original available. We made efforts to get that, we made inquiries of Mr. Fila, but he made it clear to us, in all fairness to him, from the beginning, that there was no original. Yes, we have an obligation to investigate an alibi, but I think that what this is, is so that we can put questions to alibi witnesses, so that we are not caught off guard completely when alibi witnesses come into the courtroom; that we should be able to prepare and be in a position to cross-examine them intelligently and not hear about an alibi for the first time when a witness sits down and we've had no chance to investigate what they are saying. But I don't think that the rules can be read in such a way, I would respectfully suggest, that we are required to rebut an alibi before the testimony has already been put forward. I mean, I think that if that is the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. To investigate the alibi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have attempted to investigate it, and we have. And it was during the course of this investigation that we have determined that there were alterations made to the videotape or that -- either the witnesses have been untruthful. It's one or the other. As soon as we had learned this, we have made efforts to then have this testing done, but at the point that we have made final conclusions on this, we -- until the point where we have made final conclusions that this has occurred, we weren't in a position to go forward with any testing. I mean, we will comply with the court's order to do this by June the 12th. If I can have it done before that, we certainly will.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply do not think so, if it is my duty to say that I should be presenting alibi evidence. I have given statements to the Prosecutor, and it was obvious that they were talking about a tape, and at the request of this court I gave a tape. And that is the only tape I have in my possession. That is the one that you have now. So there is not an original. There is just a mini-tape, and that's been destroyed, and you heard about this. So the copy that this court has is the one that was identified by witness Lazarevic, the copy that he gave me. So that is the original, so-to-speak, the one I had in my hands. The mother of all cassettes from which the others were made. The Prosecutor had enough time to rebut it by witnesses. I am not complaining -- let the FBI see it, let everybody else see it, but this is a technical matter, and I would not like to see another thing. And it is against the rules, to bring in new witnesses now which would prove that he was somewhere else, and something that is not related to the tape. Everything that is related to the tape is fine, but this other business, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. The issue that is here, and what determined to us that there was falsification of the tape, was at the point that a witness said that these buses were in Negoslavci. Mr. Fila had said that approximately a month ago, when he stood up and said it from the bar table, but we had no testimony to that effect. We determined where we thought this was. It was only at the point that one of his witnesses testified under oath that this was in fact in Negoslavci that we realised or that we felt that they were putting forward something which was not correct. And that's when we initiated these efforts, to make all these determinations. But we cannot be expected to anticipate what his witnesses are going to say. In all of their statements, not one person said that these buses were in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that is not a contestable point. We are not contesting that. I accept what you are saying, what you are saying now. I just do not want the witnesses to appear who could have been used earlier. And the witness that you have mentioned now, who said that they were not in Negoslavci, but in Cameroon, for example, I have got nothing against that. That is something new, novel. And I agree, and there is no difference of opinion between us. I just don't want to see a witness, for example, some other Ante Markovic or Mesic or, God knows, some other Mesic. That is what I don't want to see or hear. That's against the rules, I feel. But everything that would be evidence showing that the tape was falsified, that I falsified it, or whatever you want, that's all right. Of course I would never do that. That's all right. There is no problem with that. I am not questioning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: One other point, if I might make it, please. Before we closed our case, Mr. Niemann expressly addressed this issue to the court, and he said what had been done in the Tadic case, where there were fairly liberal rules as to what would be allowed under rebuttal. At that point we put this issue to the court, and I think, in all fairness, that if additional restrictions are being placed on us now, we should then be allowed to reopen our case, if that is the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, let me interrupt. Clearly, the position as to the tape is of crucial importance, in particular the position about where the buses were at 3.42. It would, therefore, be helpful if you were to find what references there were to that during the course, if any, of the Prosecution case, and whether it's so that the first reference to their being in Negoslavci came during the Defence case, as my recollection is. But that should be checked. But we are dealing, are we not, with an hypothesis at the moment, because we don't know what your evidence is going to be. It may be that we would be in a better position to resolve it when we know what it is, and how it is that you put the case, that this is rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a very fair assessment. Probably all sides here are not that far apart on this. We don't intend, by any means, to abuse this privilege. We want to comply with what the court has said. We want to condense this as much as possible and get it out. We are not planning on parading a whole crowd of witnesses before the court again and replaying our case. Anything that we say at this point is going to be in response to things that came in the Defence case. The bulk of it is addressed to the alibi video, and beyond that -- again, it's not going to be extensive evidence. But I agree with Your Honours' position, that you should see what we have, what we are going to present, and then everyone can talk about this in a more educated fashion, and we are not talking around issues. Honestly, at this point, I am not in a position to say exactly what we will be doing. And so I am at somewhat of a disadvantage, because I am trying to argue for factors that are not completely known to me, but not trying to put myself into a corner where, if we determine we need to do something, I have already ruled that possibility out, just out of ignorance of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. All right. I think, in any case, we will -- first of all, let us stick to this deadline which I have set. Again, for the Prosecutor, 12th of June at 12.00 p.m., everything should be turned over to the Defence in English; if possible, in Serbian. Whereas the Defence counsel has a deadline, the 15th of June. Of course, on any matter which is questionable, we reserve the right to rule on the admissibility of the evidence, of the relevant evidence, and we will do so, if objections are raised to the admissibility of evidence, of rebuttal evidence. I wonder whether we could now hear Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Waespi went just now to check on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As for the document -- the interview with Mr. Berghofer, I think it is not put in evidence, and so we will give it back to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand from Mr. Waespi that they need about five more minutes, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can't open our discussion -- hear arguments from the parties about the particular legal issue which we reserved for some time this week, for Wednesday, the one mentioned by the Defence counsel about the right of the Prosecutor to hand in -- to call witnesses without previously handing in statements and so on. I think we can probably put it off, because it would take more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you will, Your Honour. I would just like to know -- there is the possibility, and I accepted that, that the Prosecution bring witnesses without statements. For example, an officer of the prosecuting office who they've called by telephone has come down, that's all right, or, for example, like Licina and so on. But that he has the statement and that I am not given the statement, that I find unacceptable. That is the essence of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that we have done that. I think at any point where we have a statement of a Prosecution witness, we have handed that over. Perhaps it's a -- I think the issue, I think, is a Defence witness. It's a Defence witness. It's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, this was about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- the Defence witness, and you had a statement from the Defence witness, and you produced in court the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Again, in reading the Rule, it says we have an obligation to turn over witness statements of Prosecution witnesses. I know you've put off this argument, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think it goes to the whole nature of cross-examination. If we are not going to get into that at this point, I won't, but it's -- I certainly have views on that, and I think the Office of the Prosecutor does. And what we did is, in compliance with the policy that is set forth in the Rules, and what has been done in both the Tadic and the Blaskic cases. We have not veered from that policy whatsoever, and there was no precedent to us that we should have acted in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I know the position of now both the parties. We would probably try to think it over --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I just remind you of something. Additional statements taken three years ago, as with Cvetkovic, for example, I got on the very morning, whereas it was taken only three years ago. And three years later Prosecutor Williamson remembered to find it on that particular morning, and not when the indictment was raised. That's true. I want to believe you or not to believe you, but it's not -- it's not all right that things should be like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But this again is a different matter, because Cvetkovic was a Prosecution witness. So what you are claiming now, what you are arguing now, is that the witness statement should have been given you before, not the very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of course. Yes, of course. That is the crux of the issue. Both sides. Because if it is our aim here -- you know what the question is. What the aim of this hearing is, of this trial is, to determine the truth, or to hide things from one another and to see who is more intelligent, the Prosecution or the Defence, myself. That's the essence. If the object is the truth, then they can be supplied on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I take the liberty of quoting. Before we started with this trial, it struck me what one day Judge May told me, and I think he was quite wise in saying that. "In any case, in this Tribunal we should avoid trial by ambush," as he put it. And I think he is quite right. I think this is precisely what we should avoid. I mean, by all means. So therefore, in light of this basic notion, we should call upon both parties to disclose their material as soon as possible. But the particular technical issue we are discussing now was totally different; namely, to what extent the Prosecutor has the obligation to give the Defence a statement taken from a Defence witness. This was a different issue, and we have probably to reflect upon, to ponder this issue well, and we may decide to make a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would certainly like to put arguments to the court before a ruling is made, because we have very strong positions on this. And I think that, as I said, if the court rules contrary to the position that we are advocating, this is a different path than what has been accepted in our trials, and it has a great precedent effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It may not even be -- sorry to interrupt you. It may not even be important to make a ruling. I was thinking, for the sake of legal propriety and of proceeding in a proper judicial manner, to have a clear picture of the legal framework of our proceedings, but probably for our particular trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite certainly we won't be in a situation of that kind again, because we've completed our witnesses. I just wanted to have the same intention. It wasn't correct to do so. Nothing else from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, in conclusion, is just that we are not accusing Mr. Fila of acting in bad faith, and I can say to the court that we have not acted in bad faith. There are a lot of problems that revolve around witnesses, that are in other countries, that things get tied up in translation. You know, Mr. Fila in the last few days has presented us with a lot of documents at the last minute. We accept that these things are going to happen and, you know, we certainly try to comply with all the rules, but I think it's important to recognise that everyone here is acting in good faith, and this is not an intent to deceive or to ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, that's not what I said. I just want to say that it is not the level of this court to do this kind of thing to each other. As a young lawyer, of course, I was used to this in the common and municipal courts. I was president of the chamber of lawyers and I had a lawyer who swallowed one of the crucial papers in the case. We had that too. But that's not our level here. That's not up to our level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I hope that we can now hear Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have these here now, the redacted notes, so we would put these forward. First of all, the redacted notes, and then the redacted report as well, which, as I indicated, is part of a larger report, and we have taken out the only -- the portion that refers to Mr. Novakovic and have redacted all of those portions which relate to issues upon which I am not going to question him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The documents are marked Prosecution Exhibit 211 and 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Bos, what are the numbers again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: 211 being the notes and 212 being the report, the typed report?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, I'm sorry. I apologise for this delay. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry. I wonder whether Mr. Fila needed some time. Do you need some time to go through the notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While Mr. Williamson is asking his questions, I'll be able to read through them, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is very brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis where are you employed?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: For the Office of the Prosecutor at the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Are you seconded to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have been seconded since the 1st of May 1995, as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where are you seconded from the?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: From the Warwickshire constabulary in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How long have you been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Seventeen years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the course of those 17 years what type of work have you been engaged in?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: For the past 15 I have been engaged in criminal investigations, and included in that is a supervisory role with serious investigations. Investigations into serious crime, and also around the 4th intelligence bureau for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Since arriving at the Tribunal, have you been involved in the investigation of events which occurred in the Vukovar region of Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, since 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in that capacity did you have occasion to interview Ljuba Novakovic in February of this year?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances under which this interview took place? Were there a series of interviews conducted?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. From Mr. Fila's office we were given details of potential Defence witnesses, and I, with others, was involved in the interviewing of those witnesses in various locations in Croatia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where did you interview Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: In his office in Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: On the 20th of February, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you interviewed Mr. Novakovic, were you accompanied by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was this interpreter certified by the Tribunal to translate from Serbian to English and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I am aware of that, although I have not worked with her before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was anybody else present when you interviewed Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you explain to Mr. Novakovic your purpose for being there?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: In no uncertain terms I explained exactly who I was, the reason why I was there, and that we -- I wished to talk about the statement that he gave to Mr. Fila's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did he then indicate a willingness to answer your questions?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you were conducting this interview, did you make any notes as to what was being said?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. I took the notes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you use these notes to prepare a report, after you returned to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I prepared the report from the notes the following day, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you have those notes and the report in court with you today?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the course of your interview with Mr. Novakovic, did you have occasion to ask him about how often he had had contacts with Slavko Dokmanovic during the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. May I refer to my notes, Your Honours? Or, in fact, the report. On the second page of the report, I've put down what he told me; "that from about September onwards in 1991, I used to see Slavko at least every other day and on those days we did not meet. We would speak with each other on the telephone. I would go to places like Bobota, Trpinja, Vera, or wherever they needed aid. And of course I would deal mostly with Slavko, because he used to be the Mayor."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As you spoke with Mr. Novakovic, what term did he use when referring to the position that he held, and the position that Mr. Dokmanovic had held?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: He referred to them both as the Mayor. And because this term had been an issue from the outset of the arrest of Mr. Dokmanovic, I clarified that through the interpreter, and he used the term Mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Novakovic state anything to you in relation to how he viewed Mr. Dokmanovic's status as Mayor during the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes. He said that -- and again I'll quote from my notes, from the report; "I still held Slavko to be the Mayor and therefore I felt it was important to keep him informed about what was going on in the area of Ilok and the fact that some Serbs had been captured by Croatian extremists."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a moment, Mr. Williamson. If I saw this -- if I am correct, this is a report and not notes? They are not notes but a report; is that correct? Why has it been crossed out? I don't know what it says afterwards. This is an incomplete document. You can't delete things from a document. What, if on that second place it says that that is not true, what is being said at the moment? I did not give you a -- documents cut out with scissors, three sentences snipped off the top, three snipped off the bottom. This is not acceptable as a document. So I should like you to give a ruling on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We had already -- we have already ruled before, and -- on this matter. We authorised the Prosecutor to redact this document, both the handwritten notes and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The notes, he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- and the typewritten report. The Prosecutor was authorized by the Trial Chamber to redact, because there are references to other matters which are of no relevance to the particular interview with Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecutor explained that he had talked -- that Mr. Curtis had talked to seven witnesses, and that he would be deleting that, but this is the talk with Mr. Novakovic alone. Only with Mr. Novakovic. And he is crossing out part of his interview with Novakovic, which relates to Ilok and the rest. You did not bring in a ruling of that kind, to that effect. That is not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I offered to hand over the entire report. And I had indicated that I only wished to question Mr. Curtis on very limited matters where there was -- where Mr. Novakovic had denied what he said. And it was at the court's instruction that we redacted it. Again, I am happy to put in the entire report. But I think that it generally works in our favour. But the issue here was only those points which Mr. Novakovic denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Williamson is right. I mean, the ruling was that the -- since this report -- you are right, Mr. Fila, in saying that this report only deals with Mr. Dokmanovic. However, the redaction was authorized because the points which have been crossed out are points which do -- which will not be raised by Mr. Williamson in examination. So that's why. But if you insist, and on receiving the whole report, and Mr. Williamson is prepared to do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't insist. We just began with notes at the last hearing. We have come here to discuss whether we are going to get the notes or not. Instead of notes, I now get a report which I heard of this morning. Now I see that part of the report has been crossed out. But, never mind, no problem. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As I say, Mr. Fila, we have decided, so therefore, as I say, if you don't want to have the whole report which the Prosecutor -- typewritten report which --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's all right, Your Honour. Let it be. Let it be as it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let's move on, please. Yes. Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I lost where my place was in going through the questions. If I might just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We were discussing the issue of Mayor, and the witness was quoting the second paragraph on page 2, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Novakovic indicate to you any obligation that he felt, arising from the fact that he still viewed Mr. Dokmanovic as Mayor, to keep Mr. Dokmanovic informed of events that were occurring during this period.

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, and simply for that reason, because he felt that Mr. Dokmanovic was still responsible and still felt responsible for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion with Mr. Novakovic in relation to the events of October 17th, 1991, when people left Ilok, and if so, what was said in terms of Mr. Dokmanovic's role or presence?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a conversation regarding that matter. Mr. Novakovic said that he and Mr. Dokmanovic had been authorised by their two authorities to go and observe the evacuation from Ilok, and to make sure that things went smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, I would like for you now to be shown these documents which have been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibits 211 and 212. Tell me if you can identify these documents.

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I don't know which they are, but both of them -- the handwritten one are my notes that I took at the time of the interview, and the typed one is the report that I made the following day from those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And the versions that you have here in court, the notes being Prosecutor's Exhibit 211, the report being 212, have been redacted from the original version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you make these redactions?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you redact anything other than those issues not pertaining to the questions that we've discussed here today?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I did not ask that very well. What was redacted from this?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: The matters that the court said were not relevant to the questions you were going to ask today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you were present when those discussions were going on in the courtroom, were you not?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have an objection, Your Honour. I do not accept this as evidence, that this be admitted, because Mr. Dokmanovic has not been accused of anything relating to Ilok. Second, Mr. Novakovic was not asked here by me or in the cross-examination how he experienced Mr. Dokmanovic, as a Mayor, or as a football player or as anything else. That was not a question asked. And this is rebuttal evidence which is designed to show that he said something else, and that is not what is present in Mr. Novakovic's statement. The witness is used for something that he is not -- not being put forward for. And, thirdly, I would like to ask several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, you are a member of the investigating team of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I am an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In that office are you -- is it your duty to testify? I have seen you here testifying for the second time. Is your role -- is it your role to testify? There are other investigators, as far as I know, Mr. Druro, Mr. Milner. How come that you are the one testifying every time? You testified for the legitimacy of the arrest. You now come here -- is it your role in the Prosecution to come up and give testimony, to testify every time? I claim that you are giving testimony in an interested fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Bias fashion. I'm sorry, bias fashion. You say Dokmanovic is a murderer. I never raised an objection. You are speaking in that way towards the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, which language did you use in talking to Mr. Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: (Answer inaudible).

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Novakovic speaks English as well, doesn’t he?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I don't know if he speaks English, the conversation was through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who was the interpreter? Where is the interpreter? What is the interpreter's name?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the name of the interpreter being put forward. I mean, this is a policy that has been followed throughout the proceedings of this Tribunal, and these are persons who are working in the field --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well, very well. I withdraw my objection. So an interpreter exists. No, I withdraw my question as to the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So, let's say, the interpreter exists,; is that right? The interpreter existed? I am not asking you the name or anything else? There was an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: An interpreter did exist?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's all I am asking, nothing else. What you asked in English, the interpreter asked in Serbian, Mr. Novakovic answered in Serbian, and the interpreter translated for you into English, and you wrote that down in your notes, and then from the notes you drew up your report; is that right? Have I said that correctly?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you write those notes -- the report in the presence of Mr. Novakovic, or when you went wherever you went, later on?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I wrote the notes in the presence of Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. And not the report?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: The report was made the following day, in Belgrade. Mr. Novakovic was not in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. That's fine. Yes. During that time wherein you had talks in the presence of Mr. Novakovic, was that in Mr. Novakovic's office?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: The office he told me was his, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did he have a secretary?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: In an outside office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes. At some particular point did the secretary bring you any alcohol, alcoholic beverage?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I think that alcohol was offered at the beginning of the interview and there was a glass of rakija at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Not a bottle of whiskey between you and Mr. Novakovic which was full at the beginning of the talk and empty at the end of your talks?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I think that it's well-known I don't drink whiskey, and I didn't drink any other alcohol during the course of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis, I didn't say that you drank the alcohol.

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: I didn't. You implied that. I did not drink any alcohol during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No. I asked whether at the beginning of the talk the bottle of whiskey was full and whether it was empty at the end of the discussion. That's what I asked?

utterances.speaker: KEVIN CURTIS
utterances.text: There was no whiskey or any other alcohol in the room during the course of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
